questions.problem: Find the fourth-degree Taylor polynomial of ${sin}^{2}⁡(x)$ about $x=\frac{\pi }{2}.$
questions.worked_solution:
The fourth-degree Taylor polynomial of $f(x)$ about $x=a$ is given by

$$
{P}_{4}(x)=f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{{f}^{″}(a)}{2!}(x-a)^{2}+\frac{{f}^{‴}(a)}{3!}(x-a)^{3}+\frac{{f}^{(4)}(a)}{4!}(x-a)^{4}.
$$

Here, we have $a=\frac{\pi }{2},$ so

$$
{P}_{4}(x)=f(\frac{\pi }{2})+{f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2})(x-\frac{\pi }{2})+\frac{{f}^{″}(\frac{\pi }{2})}{2!}{(x-\frac{\pi }{2})}^{2}+\frac{{f}^{‴}(\frac{\pi }{2})}{3!}{(x-\frac{\pi }{2})}^{3}+\frac{{f}^{(4)}(\frac{\pi }{2})}{4!}{(x-\frac{\pi }{2})}^{4}.
$$

So we need to work out $f(\frac{\pi }{2}),$ ${f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2}),$ ${f}^{″}(\frac{\pi }{2}),$ ${f}^{‴}(\frac{\pi }{2})$ and ${f}^{(4)}(\frac{\pi }{2}),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ={sin}^{2}⁡(x) & ⟹ &  & f(\frac{\pi }{2}) & ={sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})=1 \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x) & ⟹ &  & {f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi }{2})=0 \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x) & ⟹ &  & {f}^{″}(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{2\pi }{2})=-2 \\ {f}^{‴}(x) & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x) & ⟹ &  & {f}^{‴}(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi }{2})=0 \\ {f}^{(4)}(x) & =-8\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x) & ⟹ &  & {f}^{(4)}(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =-8\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{2\pi }{2})=8\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${P}_{4}(x)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{4}(x) & =1+(0)(x-\frac{\pi }{2})+(\frac{(-2)}{2!}){(x-\frac{\pi }{2})}^{2}+\frac{0}{3!}{(x-\frac{\pi }{2})}^{3}+\frac{8}{4!}{(x-\frac{\pi }{2})}^{4} \\  & =1-{(x-\frac{\pi }{2})}^{2}+\frac{1}{3}{(x-\frac{\pi }{2})}^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the fourth-degree Taylor polynomial of $-\operatorname{sin}⁡x$ about $x=\frac{\pi }{2}.$
questions.worked_solution:
The fourth-degree Taylor polynomial of $f(x)$ about $x=a$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{4}(x) & =f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{{f}^{″}(a)}{2!}(x-a)^{2}+\frac{{f}^{‴}(a)}{3!}(x-a)^{3}+\frac{{f}^{⁗}(a)}{4!}(x-a)^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have $a=\frac{\pi }{2},$ so

$$
{P}_{4}(x)=f(\frac{\pi }{2})+{f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2})(x-\frac{\pi }{2})+\frac{{f}^{″}(\frac{\pi }{2})}{2!}{(x-\frac{\pi }{2})}^{2}+\frac{{f}^{‴}(\frac{\pi }{2})}{3!}{(x-\frac{\pi }{2})}^{3}+\frac{{f}^{(4)}(\frac{\pi }{2})}{4!}{(x-\frac{\pi }{2})}^{4}.
$$

So we need to work out $f(\frac{\pi }{2}),$ ${f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2}),$ ${f}^{″}(\frac{\pi }{2}),$ ${f}^{‴}(\frac{\pi }{2})$ and ${f}^{(4)}(\frac{\pi }{2}),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡(x) & ⟹ &  & f(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})=-1 \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡(x) & ⟹ &  & {f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})=0 \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(x) & ⟹ &  & {f}^{″}(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})=1 \\ {f}^{‴}(x) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(x) & ⟹ &  & {f}^{‴}(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})=0 \\ {f}^{(4)}(x) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡(x) & ⟹ &  & {f}^{(4)}(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})=-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${P}_{4}(x)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{4}(x) & =-1+0(x-\frac{\pi }{2})+\frac{1}{2!}{(x-\frac{\pi }{2})}^{2}+\frac{0}{3!}{(x-\frac{\pi }{2})}^{3}+(-\frac{1}{4!}){(x-\frac{\pi }{2})}^{4} \\  & =-1+\frac{1}{2}{(x-\frac{\pi }{2})}^{2}-\frac{1}{24}{(x-\frac{\pi }{2})}^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Obtaining a Higher-Order Derivative Of a Function Given its Higher-Degree Taylor Polynomial
questions.problem:
The fourth-degree Taylor polynomial of $f(x)$ about $x=0$ is given by

$$
{P}_{4}(x)=x-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}-\frac{1}{4}{x}^{4}.
$$

What is ${f}^{(4)}(0)?$
questions.worked_solution:
The coefficient of ${x}^{4}$ is given by $\frac{{f}^{(4)}(0)}{4!}.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{f}^{(4)}(0)}{4!} & =-\frac{1}{4} \\ \frac{{f}^{(4)}(0)}{24} & =-\frac{1}{4} \\ {f}^{(4)}(0) & =-6.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
The fourth-degree Taylor polynomial of $f(x)$ about $x=2$ is given by

$$
{P}_{4}(x)=1+2(x-2)+2(x-2)^{2}+\frac{4}{3}(x-2)^{3}+\frac{2}{3}(x-2)^{4}.
$$

What is ${f}^{‴}(2)?$
questions.worked_solution:
The coefficient of $(x-2)^{3}$ is given by $\frac{{f}^{‴}(2)}{3!}.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{f}^{‴}(2)}{3!} & =\frac{4}{3} \\ \frac{{f}^{‴}(2)}{6} & =\frac{4}{3} \\ {f}^{‴}(2) & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

The fourth-degree Taylor polynomial of $f(x)$ about $x=2$ is given by

$$
{P}_{4}(x)=-4-12(x-2)-5(x-2)^{2}-2(x-2)^{3}+(x-2)^{4}.
$$

What is ${f}^{(4)}(2)?$
questions.worked_solution:
The coefficient of $(x-2)^{4}$ is given by $\frac{{f}^{(4)}(2)}{4!}.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{f}^{(4)}(2)}{4!} & =1 \\ \frac{{f}^{(4)}(2)}{24} & =1 \\ {f}^{(4)}(2) & =24.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
The fourth-degree Taylor polynomial of $f(x)$ about $x=-2$ is given by

$$
{P}_{4}(x)=35-60(x+2)+40(x+2)^{2}-11(x+2)^{3}+(x+2)^{4}.
$$

What is ${f}^{‴}(-2)?$
questions.worked_solution:
The coefficient of $(x+2)^{3}$ is given by $\frac{{f}^{‴}(-2)}{3!}.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{f}^{‴}(-2)}{3!} & =-11 \\ \frac{{f}^{‴}(-2)}{6} & =-11 \\ {f}^{‴}(-2) & =-66.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Let $f(x) = \sin{x}.$ Calculate the fourth-degree Taylor polynomial for $f(x)$ about $x=\dfrac{\pi}{2}.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The fourth-degree Taylor polynomial of $f(x)$ about $x=a$ is given by

$$
P_4(x) = f(a) + f'(a)(x-a) + \dfrac{f''(a)}{2!}(x-a)^2 + \dfrac{f'''(a)}{3!}(x-a)^3 + \dfrac{f^{(4)}(a)}{4!}(x-a)^4.
$$

Here, we have $a=\dfrac{\pi}{2},$ so

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{4}(x) & =f(\frac{\pi }{2})+{f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2})(x-\frac{\pi }{2})+\frac{{f}^{″}(\frac{\pi }{2})}{2!}{(x-\frac{\pi }{2})}^{2} \\  & \,\,\,\,+\frac{{f}^{‴}(\frac{\pi }{2})}{3!}{(x-\frac{\pi }{2})}^{3}+\frac{{f}^{(4)}(\frac{\pi }{2})}{4!}{(x-\frac{\pi }{2})}^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

So we need to work out $f\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right),$ $f'\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right),$ $f''\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right),$ $f'''\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$ and $f^{(4)}\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x & ⟹ &  & f(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =1 \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x & ⟹ &  & {f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =0 \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡x & ⟹ &  & {f}^{″}(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =-1 \\ {f}^{‴}(x) & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡x & ⟹ &  & {f}^{‴}(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =0 \\ {f}^{(4)}(x) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x & ⟹ &  & {f}^{(4)}(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $P_4(x)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{4}(x) & =1-\frac{1}{2!}{(x-\frac{\pi }{2})}^{2}+\frac{1}{4!}{(x-\frac{\pi }{2})}^{4} \\  & =1-\frac{1}{2}{(x-\frac{\pi }{2})}^{2}+\frac{1}{24}{(x-\frac{\pi }{2})}^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
The fourth-degree Taylor polynomial of $f(x)$ about $x=0$ is given by

$$
P_4(x) = 1+2x-3x^2+4x^3-5x^4.
$$

What is $f^{(4)}(0)?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The coefficient of $x^4$ is given by $\dfrac{f^{(4)}(0)}{4!}.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{f}^{(4)}(0)}{4!} & =-5 \\ \frac{{f}^{(4)}(0)}{24} & =-5 \\ {f}^{(4)}(0) & =-120.\end{aligned}
$$
